A_target.statement:
Let $f: \hointr 1 \infty \to \R_{>0}$ be [[Definition:Decreasing Real Function|decreasing]].
Then:
:$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^\infty \map f n$ [[Definition:Convergent Series|converges]] {{iff}} $\displaystyle \int_1^\infty \map f x \rd x$ converges

B_source.statement:
Let $f$ be [[Definition:Decreasing Real Function|decreasing]] on $\closedint n {n + 1}$.
Then:
:$\displaystyle \map f {n + 1} \le \int_n^{n + 1} \map f x \rd x \le \map f n$

substitutions.the integral over [n, n+1]: a term sandwiched between f(n+1) and f(n)

derived.sum of the sandwich bounds: partial sums bounding the integral above and below
derived.boundedness of one side: boundedness of the other, hence joint convergence

object_map.reformulation: Approximate the integral by unit-width rectangles under and over the curve, so the series and integral bound each other.

validity_conditions: f positive and decreasing gives f(n+1) <= integral_n^{n+1} f <= f(n) on each unit interval.
Summing over n, the partial sums of the series and the truncated integrals differ by at most f(1), so one is bounded iff the other is.
Monotone bounded sequences converge, so the series and integral converge together.
proof_plan:
On $\closedint n {n + 1}$, by the source result:
:$\displaystyle \map f {n + 1} \le \int_n^{n + 1} f \le \map f n$

Summing for $n = 1, \ldots, N - 1$:
:$\displaystyle \sum_{n \mathop = 2}^N \map f n \le \int_1^N f \le \sum_{n \mathop = 1}^{N - 1} \map f n$

As $f > 0$, the partial sums and $\displaystyle \int_1^N f$ are increasing in $N$.
By the inequalities, one is bounded {{iff}} the other is.
